prompt: English has become the main language of international business, science and travel. Some people see this as a practical advantage, while others believe it threatens smaller languages and the cultures attached to them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
The spread of English as a common working language has been one of the most visible effects of globalisation. Supporters point to the practical convenience it creates, while others fear that smaller languages are being displaced along with the cultures they carry. I accept the value of a shared language but believe the concern about displacement is well founded.

The advantages are substantial and easy to demonstrate. A single working language allows a Brazilian engineer and a Korean supplier to negotiate without either learning the other's language, and it gives researchers access to the great majority of published work in their field. Students, too, gain entry to institutions that would otherwise be closed to them. The alternative is not a world of equal multilingualism but a world of slower and more expensive translation.

The risk to smaller languages is nevertheless real, and it operates through incentives rather than prohibition. Nobody bans a minority language; parents simply calculate that their children's prospects depend on the dominant one and stop passing theirs on. Within two generations a language can move from ordinary domestic use to something spoken only at funerals. What is lost with it is not only vocabulary but forms of classification — for plants, for weather, for kinship — that took centuries to develop. A language that has stopped being spoken at home cannot be revived by teaching it as a school subject.

My position is that both effects are genuine and that they are not symmetrical. The convenience of English is enormous but reversible, since a world that stopped using it would simply adopt something else. The disappearance of a language is permanent. That asymmetry is why I would support serious public investment in minority-language education, even while continuing to teach English to everyone.
title: English as a world language
